c.tagline: Morocco's relaxed ocean capital of kasbahs, gardens and storks.

taxi.fareNote: Rabat's blue petits taxis are metered and cheap for up to three passengers within the city, so insist on the meter (compteur). Careem also operates via app, and beige grands taxis run fixed shared intercity routes.

emergency.note: Dial 19 for police in cities, 15 for medical/SAMU, and 177 for the Gendarmerie Royale outside urban areas.

avoid.reason: No true no-go areas; at most avoid deserted medina lanes and the beach/corniche late at night.
Mind pickpockets in the medina, at Rabat-Ville station and in market crowds, and politely decline unofficial 'guides'.

hood_desc: Rabat's walled old town, gentler and more orderly than those of Fes or Marrakech, with a straight souk street of textiles and crafts running down toward the ocean and the Kasbah of the Udayas at its northern edge; atmospheric riads and easy sightseeing.

The monumental government quarter of grand boulevards, home to the Hassan Tower and the Mausoleum of Mohammed V, close to the tram and train station; a central, dignified base within walking distance of the medina.
Rabat's fashionable modern district of tree-lined avenues, cafes, bars, boutiques and restaurants popular with students and young professionals; the city's go-to area for dining and nightlife.
The French-built new town of orderly Art Deco boulevards centred on Avenue Mohammed V, with hotels, offices and the main train station; a convenient, walkable heart of the modern city.
A leafy, upscale residential suburb of villas, embassies and luxury hotels south of the centre; calm, green and exclusive, better for a quiet stay than for being in the thick of things.

water.note: City tap water is treated and generally safe, though many visitors prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: The tramway runs roughly 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM (later on weekends); buses cover similar hours with reduced late-night service.
transit.note: The modern Rabat-Sale tramway has two lines (L1 and L2) linking Rabat with Sale across the Bouregreg, complemented by an Alsa-run city bus and trambus network; petits taxis fill in for door-to-door trips.
transit.pay: Tram tickets (around 7 MAD) are bought from platform machines and validated on board; a single ticket allows intermodal transfer to Bus Line 30. Taxis and buses are paid in cash.

transit.m: City bus toward central Rabat (~30-40 min)
Petit/grand taxi to the city center (15-20 min, ~150 MAD fixed)

tip.r: Customary; leave ~10% at restaurants, round up taxi fares and tip cafe waiters a few dirhams.

food.name: Tagine
food.desc: Slow-cooked in a conical clay pot: chicken with preserved lemon and olives, or beef with prunes and almonds, mopped up with round khobz bread.

places.name: Dar Rbatia
places.note: Open since 1989 in an 18th-century riad, serving the full traditional Rbati repertoire in tiled salons.

places.name: Dar Zaki
places.note: Restored riad widely rated the best traditional table in Rabat, strong on tagines and pastilla.

places.name: Dar Naji
places.note: Popular local chain doing upscale-but-traditional Moroccan food, famous for its tea pouring.

food.name: Grilled seafood by the Kasbah
food.desc: Sardines, sole, prawns and calamari straight off the Bou Regreg boats, grilled plain with cumin, salt and a wedge of lemon.

places.name: Borj Eddar
places.note: Terrace restaurant right on the beach beneath the Kasbah walls; grilled fish with an Atlantic view.

places.name: Le Dhow
places.note: Converted wooden boat moored on the river, a striking setting for seafood and sunset.

places.name: Restaurant de la Plage
places.note: The anchor address for seafood on the beach front, best at sunny weekend lunch.

food.name: Rfissa
food.desc: Shredded msemen or trid pastry soaked in a fenugreek, saffron and ras el hanout broth under chicken and lentils - a family celebration dish.

places.name: Dar Naji
places.note: Locals recommend its mini-trid version of rfissa, available affordably and without ordering ahead.

places.name: Dar Rbatia
places.note: Cooks rfissa, tanjia and mechoui on request if you give the kitchen advance notice.

places.name: Dar Zaki
places.note: Riad kitchen that will prepare the more elaborate home dishes for groups on request.

food.name: Pastilla
food.desc: Layers of paper-thin warqa pastry over pigeon or chicken with almonds and cinnamon, dusted with icing sugar - sweet and savoury at once.

places.name: Dar Zaki
places.note: Its pastilla is singled out in recent guides as the best version in the capital.

places.name: Dar Rbatia
places.note: Serves pastilla as part of a full traditional menu in a richly decorated riad.

places.name: Dar Naji
places.note: Reliable, busy and open late, with pastilla on the standard menu rather than by request.

food.name: Chebakia and Moroccan pastries
food.desc: Sesame dough flowers fried and steeped in honey, plus ghriba shortbread, kaab el ghzal and briouates - everywhere, and heaviest in Ramadan.

places.name: Patisserie Majestic
places.note: Long-established Rabat patisserie mixing French and Moroccan sweets; good boxes to take away.

places.name: Rue Souika stalls
places.note: The medina's main artery is lined with sweet sellers weighing chebakia and ghriba by the kilo.

places.name: Cafe Maure
places.note: Serves ghriba almond cakes with mint tea on terraces above the river mouth.

food.name: Harira and bissara
food.desc: Tomato, lentil and chickpea soup thickened with flour, or bissara - a thick split-pea puree finished with olive oil and cumin, eaten for breakfast.

places.name: Rue Souika soup counters
places.note: Standing counters serve bissara from dawn for a few dirhams with bread and olive oil.

places.name: Dar Naji
places.note: Does a sit-down version of harira alongside the rest of the traditional menu.

places.name: Marche central
places.note: Market cafes near the produce halls serve soup and grilled skewers at lunchtime.

food.name: Mint tea
food.desc: Green gunpowder tea steeped with a fistful of spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from height to build a head of foam. Say atay bi naanaa.

places.name: Cafe Maure
places.note: Terraces in the Andalusian gardens overlooking the Bou Regreg; the classic Rabat tea stop.

places.name: Dar Naji
places.note: Known for its theatrical high-pour tea service at the table.

places.name: Rue des Consuls cafes
places.note: Cafes along the carpet-sellers' street pour tea all afternoon between browsing sessions.

food.name: Avocado smoothie and fresh orange juice
food.desc: Avocado blended with milk, almonds and dates into a thick shake, or orange juice pressed to order - the everyday non-alcoholic staples.

places.name: Juice stalls, Rue Souika
places.note: Rows of counters press oranges and blend avocado shakes to order, very cheap.

places.name: Avenue Mohammed V juice bars
places.note: Cafes along the main boulevard do orange juice and avocat by the glass all day.

places.name: Marche central
places.note: Juice counters beside the market use fruit bought a few metres away.

landmarks: Hassan Tower
The 44-metre minaret of an unfinished 12th-century mosque, rising over a forest of shattered columns as Rabat's defining monument.
Mausoleum of Mohammed V
A masterpiece of modern Alaouite architecture in white marble and green tile, sheltering the tombs of the king and his sons under royal guard.
Kasbah of the Udayas
A blue-and-white walled citadel above the Bou Regreg estuary, entered through a monumental Almohad gate and ending at ocean-view ramparts.
Andalusian Gardens
A fragrant walled garden inside the kasbah, planted in the early 1900s with orange trees, bougainvillea and roaming cats beside a historic palace museum.
Chellah
A romantically ruined necropolis where storks nest atop a Roman town and Merinid sanctuary, wrapped in gardens outside the Almohad walls.
Medina of Rabat and Rue des Consuls
A relaxed 17th-century Andalusian-built quarter whose carpet and leather souks along Rue des Consuls invite haggle-free browsing.
Royal Palace (Dar al-Makhzen)
The vast ceremonial seat of the Moroccan monarchy, its manicured mechouar esplanade and gates offering a glimpse of royal grandeur.
Mohammed VI Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art
Morocco's flagship modern-art museum, a gleaming white showcase of the nation's twentieth-century masters and international exhibitions.
Grand Théâtre de Rabat
Zaha Hadid's swooping riverside opera house on the Bou Regreg, a futuristic icon of the capital's ambitious cultural renaissance.
Rabat Lighthouse and Udayas Corniche
A whitewashed 1920 lighthouse on the Atlantic point where surfers ride the breaks and sunset turns the ramparts gold.

train.note: No international trains. Rabat is on the Al Boraq high-speed line, with Tangier about 1h20 away and Casablanca 50 minutes, plus conventional services to Fes, Meknes and Marrakech. Rabat-Ville station is right in the middle of town, which makes the train much more convenient than flying for domestic trips. Book on the ONCF site or app.

bus.note: International coaches cross by ferry at Tanger Med and take a day or more into Spain. Domestically CTM and Supratours (https://www.supratours.ma/) run from the Kamra bus station south of the centre, though the train beats the bus on almost every Moroccan route from Rabat. Carry your passport for cross-border services.

ferry.note: Rabat sits at the mouth of the Bou Regreg, but the river bar makes it unusable for commercial shipping and there is no scheduled ferry. Small rowing boats cross to Salé from the kasbah - a two-minute local hop. All Morocco-Spain sailings are from the northern ports.

half.name: Casablanca
half.blurb: Morocco's largest city is about an hour south and centers on the Hassan II Mosque, one of the largest mosques in the world.

half.name: Meknes
half.blurb: An imperial city roughly two hours away preserves massive gates, granaries, and stables built during the reign of Sultan Moulay Ismail.

half.name: Moulay Bousselham
half.blurb: A coastal lagoon village about an hour and a quarter north draws birdwatchers to wetlands that serve as a wintering ground for flamingos.

full.name: Volubilis
full.blurb: The ruins of a Roman provincial capital lie about two hours away, with mosaic floors, a triumphal arch, and a basilica standing among olive groves.
